facts.claim: "One Time" is the opening track of Marian Hill's EP Sway, released 17 February 2015 on Photo Finish / Republic Records. It runs 3:37.
Jeremy Lloyd and Samantha Gongol (Samantha Lee Gongol) are credited as the writers and composers of "One Time". The publisher is Universal Music Publishing Group.
Jeremy Lloyd is the duo's producer. He has produced and mixed in Propellerhead Reason since the start, and Sway was mixed entirely in Reason.

Saxophonist Steve Davit joined the duo for a Rolling Stone live session performance of "One Time". Rolling Stone described the song as bluesy and speakeasy-like, and said it had become a popular soundtrack for Vine videos.

Jeremy Lloyd said "One Time" appeared in a big Vine, and that it was the song everyone sang along to when the duo began playing shows. He said it grew from a bubble of influencers and an organic groundswell.
Samantha Gongol called "One Time" one of her favorites to perform. She said it was the first of their songs to gain popularity.
The song is a first-person lyric about a woman who says she isn't "the kind of drum you play one time". It is a statement about not being used and discarded.
"One Time" is listed in Marian Hill's discography as a 2015 single from Sway, with an RIAA Gold certification and a chart peak of 38.

Marian Hill is a Philadelphia duo of singer Samantha Gongol and producer Jeremy Lloyd. Their debut single "Whisky" came out in 2013, and their first full-length, Act One (2016), included the Top 30 single "Down".
Lloyd sent the first song, "Whisky", blindly to music blogs, and the duo then signed to Photo Finish/Republic Records. Press describes their sound as a mix of 1920s jazz and electronica.

research.lineage: The song sits in a Philadelphia/Brooklyn strand of left-field pop and alternative R&B that fuses sparse electronic beats with jazz and blues saxophone and chopped, sultry vocals.

draft:
The whole song hangs on one odd, perfect metaphor. **One Time** doesn't use the usual figures for being loved and left, the toy or the game or the notch on a bedpost. Samantha Gongol picks an instrument: "But I'm not the kind of drum you play one time." A drum is built to be hit, and she doesn't pretend otherwise. She isn't refusing the attention. She's refusing the brevity. The line is half warning and half invitation, and it lands as both every time it comes back around, which is often.

The verses are built as a mirror. The first one sizes him up: the charm that "makes the girls all swing," the taste for the hit and run, the knowing. The second flips every pronoun. Now it's "I know," her sway, her read on "the way that men can be." Then comes the line that gives the game away: "I like it smooth and slow, give it some time to grow." Under the poise is plain want. She wants something that lasts, and she says so.

That's what keeps the song from being a simple kiss-off. The refrain opens with "Boy, if you wanna go I would not mind," which is a shrug, and a shrug repeated a dozen times stops looking like indifference. Pride and longing sit in the same breath and never settle. She'll let him leave. She just needs him to know what he's leaving. The song understands that you can mean both halves at once.

Jeremy Lloyd, the duo's producer, keeps the record almost bare. A simple, staccato synth bass and a drum machine set up a steady hip-hop groove, and the mix is clean and dry, close enough to feel like a room with the door shut. Gongol's voice is clear and breathy. She half-raps the verses with a melodic lilt, then stacks her own voice on the hook so "one time" comes back doubled. Sway was mixed entirely in Propellerhead Reason, and the restraint shows. Nothing is there that the vocal doesn't need.

The lyric's back half is where that restraint pays off. The words splinter into stuttered "pl-pl-play" and long runs of "one, one, one," the phrase chopped until it turns into rhythm. Here the singer becomes the drum. Press tied the Philadelphia duo to a meeting of 1920s jazz and electronica. Rolling Stone heard this song as bluesy and speakeasy-like, and for its live session they brought in saxophonist Steve Davit. It was the first Marian Hill song to catch on, carried by a big Vine and by crowds who sang it back at early shows, and it later went Gold.

It sticks because it lets you be cool and hungry in the same line, and saying "one time" over and over turns into a quiet way of asking for more.
